text_html: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician's office because of impotence for the past 6 months. He also has a history of pain in his calves when walking, which subsides with rest. He has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 24 years and has smoked ½ pack of cigarettes daily for the past 20 years. Erections occur in the morning when he awakens with a full bladder, but they are not firm enough to allow penetration during intercourse. His testicles are of normal size without masses, and his prostate is symmetric and slightly enlarged. Dorsalis pedis pulses are diminished bilaterally. Other pulses are normal. Examination of the lower extremities shows brawny discoloration of the skin consistent with venous stasis dermatitis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his impotence?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: The patient in this case is presenting with symptoms and risk factors for peripheral vascular disease. The most likely cause of this patient’s impotence is arterial insufficiency.

Evaluation: Peripheral vascular disease may present with symptoms of claudication, leg pain that occurs following exertion and improves with rest, decreased peripheral pulses, and erectile dysfunction.

Definition: Peripheral vascular disease is common among older male patients who have a significant smoking history and a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hyperlipidemia. The diagnosis is suggested by absent or diminished peripheral pulses, hairless legs with smooth skin that may ulcerate, and is further supported by a reduced ankle brachial index. CT scan, MRI, or conventional angiography can confirm the presence of arterial stenosis and atherosclerosis of the extremities.

Prevention: The risk for developing peripheral vascular disease can be decreased through the avoidance of smoking, eating a healthy diet, and with adequate blood pressure control.

Treatment: Engaging in a walking program is a first-line therapy along with mitigation of risk factors. Additional therapeutic options include cilostazol and surgical revascularization (eg, bypass, stenting).

Differential: The patient in this case with a history of long-standing type 1 diabetes mellitus as well as cigarette smoking has been found to have brawny discoloration of the lower extremities with venous stasis dermatitis and decreased dorsalis pedis pulses. These findings indicate a likely diagnosis of peripheral vascular disease. Arterial insufficiency in cases of peripheral vascular disease can lead to the development of erectile dysfunction.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Prostate inflammation is incorrect. Prostatitis may present with dysuria, frequency, and urinary urgency similar to a urinary tract infection. On examination, a tender, boggy, enlarged prostate can be palpated.

Choice C: Psychogenic sexual dysfunction is incorrect. Psychogenic sexual dysfunction may be considered if the patient has concerns regarding erectile dysfunction but continues to have erections while sleeping. In this case, the patient does have morning erections, but they are not firm enough to allow for penetration during intercourse, making another cause more likely.

Choice D: Testosterone deficiency is incorrect. Symptoms of testosterone deficiency include decreased endurance, fatigue, depression, decreased motivation, impaired memory, infertility, and decreased sex drive. The signs and symptoms in this case are more likely due to underlying peripheral vascular disease.

Choice E: Venous incompetence is incorrect. Venous incompetence may present with lower extremity edema, varicose veins, hyperpigmentation, and venous ulcerations. The patient in this case has been found to have decreased dorsalis pedis pulses with symptoms of claudication, which make arterial insufficiency more likely.
